first-law-s1.title: A sign hung from two cords
first-law-s1.text: A 5.0 kg sign hangs at rest from two identical light cords. Each cord makes a 30° angle with the horizontal. Use g = 9.8 m/s².

first-law-s2.title: A crate pushed across a warehouse floor
first-law-s2.text: A worker pushes a 40 kg crate across a level floor with a horizontal force. A motion detector records the crate's velocity, and a force sensor between the worker's hands and the crate records the push. The friction from the floor is 120 N throughout. At 2.0 s the worker starts pushing harder.

table.caption: Push and velocity of the crate

items.q: What is the size of the upward pull that the two cords together exert on the sign, in newtons?

mistakes.why: Value: 5.0 is the mass in kg. The cords must balance the weight, mg.

why.correct: The sign is at rest, so the net force on it is zero. Together the cords pull up exactly as hard as Earth pulls down: mg = 5.0 kg × 9.8 m/s² = 49 N.

items.q: What is the tension in each cord, in newtons?

mistakes.why: Value: that splits the weight evenly between the cords as if they were vertical. Each cord pulls at 30° above the horizontal, so only F_T sin 30° of each pull is upward.
Value: that uses cos 30°. The vertical component of a pull at 30° above the horizontal is F_T sin 30°.

why.correct: Vertically, the two upward components balance the weight: 2F_T sin 30° = mg, so F_T = mg ÷ (2 sin 30°) = 49 N ÷ (2 × 0.50) = 49 N. Each cord pulls with 49 N, more than half the weight, because only part of each pull is upward.

items.q: Why do the horizontal pulls of the two cords on the sign cancel?
options: Equal tensions at equal angles pull equally hard to opposite sides
The cords pull up, and horizontal pulls do not affect a hanging sign
The weight of the sign cancels the horizontal pulls
The ceiling pushes sideways on the sign to cancel them

why.correct: The left cord pulls up and to the left, the right cord up and to the right. With equal tensions and equal angles, the sideways parts F_T cos 30° are equal and opposite, so the horizontal net force is zero, as it must be for a sign at rest.
options: Right: equal tensions, equal angles, opposite sideways parts.
Each cord does pull partly sideways; those parts cancel each other rather than having no effect.
The weight points straight down, so it cannot cancel a horizontal force.
The ceiling touches the cords, not the sign; the only forces on the sign are the two cords and Earth.

items.q: The cords are replaced by longer ones attached farther apart, so each makes a smaller angle (15°) with the horizontal. The sign still hangs at rest. How does the tension in each cord change?
options: It increases, since less of each pull is upward
It decreases, since the cords are longer
It stays the same, since the weight is the same
It increases, since the sign's weight increases

why.correct: The cords still hold up the same 49 N. Each cord's upward part is F_T sin θ, and sin 15° is smaller than sin 30°, so each cord must pull harder: F_T = mg ÷ (2 sin 15°) ≈ 95 N.
options: Right: a flatter cord needs a larger tension for the same upward pull.
The length of the cord does not set the tension; the angle does.
The total upward pull is the same, but each cord gives less of its tension upward, so the tension rises.
The weight, mg, does not change when the cords change.

items.q: Which free-body diagram is correct for the sign?
options: Three arrows: two cord tensions up and outward, and F_g down
Five arrows: two tensions plus their horizontal and vertical parts
Two arrows: one total tension up and F_g down
Three arrows: two tensions and a net force arrow down

why.correct: Each cord is a separate agent, so each gets one whole arrow along its cord, plus the weight from Earth. Components belong in your equations beside the diagram, not on it, and the net force (zero here) is never an arrow.
options: Right: one whole arrow per agent.
Drawing components as extra arrows double-counts each pull; the exam does not accept components on a free-body diagram.
Two cords are two agents and two forces; merging them hides their directions.
The net force is the sum of the arrows, not an arrow of its own, and here it is zero.

items.q: Between 0.0 s and 2.0 s, what is the net force on the crate?
options: Zero
120 N forward
240 N forward
120 N backward

why.correct: The push (120 N forward) and the friction (120 N backward) balance, so the net force is zero. The table agrees: the velocity stays 0.80 m/s, constant.
options: Right: balanced forces, constant velocity.
120 N is the push alone; the friction pulls back just as hard.
This adds the sizes of two forces that point in opposite directions.
120 N is the friction alone; the push cancels it.

items.q: A student claims: "Between 0.0 s and 2.0 s the worker must push harder than the friction, or the crate would stop." Which evidence from the table best refutes this?
options: Push equals friction while v stays 0.80 m/s
The push rises to 150 N after 2.0 s
No velocity in the table is zero
The crate's mass stays 40 kg

why.correct: The first law says zero net force keeps the velocity constant, and the data show exactly that: with push = friction = 120 N, the crate keeps moving at 0.80 m/s. A moving object needs no net force to keep moving.
options: Right: balanced forces, steady motion, in the same rows of data.
The change at 3.0 s shows what an unbalanced force does, but it does not test the claim about 0.0 s to 2.0 s.
The crate never stopping is consistent with the claim and with the first law alike, so it does not decide between them.
The mass tells you how hard it is to change the velocity, not whether a net force is needed to keep it.

items.q: What happens to the crate's velocity after 2.0 s, and why?
options: It increases, because the push now exceeds the friction
It stays constant, because the crate is already moving
It increases, because any push makes a crate speed up
It decreases, because the friction now exceeds the push

why.correct: At 150 N the push is larger than the 120 N friction, so the net force is 30 N forward and the velocity grows: 0.80 → 1.55 → 2.30 m/s.
options: Right: an unbalanced forward force speeds the crate up.
Constant velocity needs zero net force; now the forces are unbalanced.
The 120 N push before 2.0 s did not speed the crate up; only a net force does.
The friction stays at 120 N, less than the 150 N push.

items.q: The worker pushes with 150 N for the rest of the trip, then lets go at 6.0 s. Immediately after letting go, what is the net force on the crate, in newtons? Give its size.

mistakes.why: Value: 30 N was the net force while the worker pushed. After letting go there is no push at all.
Value: the push stops when the hands leave the crate; a crate does not keep the force it was given.

why.correct: Once the hands leave the crate the push is gone. The only horizontal force left is the 120 N friction, backward, so the net force is 120 N backward and the crate slows down.

items.q: According to Newton's first law, an object with zero net force on it
options: keeps a constant velocity
slows down and finally stops
stays at rest whatever happens
speeds up at a slow, steady rate

why.correct: Zero net force means no change in velocity: an object at rest stays at rest, and a moving object keeps the same speed and direction.
options: Right: translational equilibrium means constant velocity.
Things on Earth slow down because friction is a net force; with zero net force nothing slows.
Moving at a constant velocity is also zero net force.
Speeding up is a change of velocity, which needs a net force.

items.q: A car drives along a straight, level highway at a steady 25 m/s. Which is true of the forces on the car?
options: The road's forward push balances the resistance
The road's forward push exceeds the resistance
There are no horizontal forces, since the speed is steady
The engine's force on the car balances the car's weight

why.correct: Steady speed in a straight line is constant velocity, so the net force is zero: forward and backward forces are equal.
options: Right: balanced horizontal forces.
A larger forward force would make the car speed up.
The forces are there; they just add to zero. Without the road's push the air would slow the car.
The weight is vertical and is balanced by the normal force; horizontal forces balance each other.

items.q: Which objects are in translational equilibrium? Select all that apply.
options: A book resting on a desk
A car pulling away from a stop sign
A ball at the top of its flight, momentarily at rest
A car rounding a curve at a steady 20 m/s

why.correct: Translational equilibrium means zero net force, so a constant velocity: same speed and same direction.
options: Right: at rest and staying at rest.
Its speed is increasing, so the forces on it do not balance.
For an instant its velocity is zero, but gravity is still the only force, so its velocity keeps changing.
Its direction changes on the curve, so its velocity changes; the net force is not zero.

items.q: A passenger on a bus moving at constant velocity drops a coin. Where does it land, relative to the point directly below her hand?
options: Directly below her hand
Behind that point, toward the back of the bus
Ahead of that point, toward the front
Behind or ahead, depending on the bus's speed

why.correct: The bus moves at constant velocity, so it is an inertial frame. The coin already moves forward with the bus and nothing pushes it horizontally while it falls, so it keeps pace with the bus and lands straight below the hand.
options: Right: no horizontal force, so the coin keeps the bus's horizontal velocity.
That would need the coin to lose its forward velocity, which takes a backward force; air resistance is negligible for a coin.
Nothing pushes the coin forward faster than the bus.
At any constant velocity the coin keeps up with the bus; only a change in the bus's velocity would matter.

items.q: A bus brakes hard, and a ball on the floor rolls toward the front. A rider says a force pushed the ball forward. What is the better explanation?
options: The ball kept its velocity while the bus slowed under it
The bus's floor pushed the ball forward during braking
The air inside the bus pushed the ball forward
The ball's inertia is a forward force acting on it

why.correct: A braking bus is accelerating, so it is not an inertial frame. Seen from the road, the ball simply keeps its velocity (first law) while the bus slows down beneath it. No forward force acts on the ball.
options: Right: the ball keeps its velocity; the bus is the one that changes.
The floor is nearly frictionless for a rolling ball and cannot push it forward while braking.
Air in a closed bus does not push the ball forward.
Inertia is a property of the ball (its mass resisting a change in velocity), not a force on it.

items.q: A 60 kg skydiver falls at a steady speed. What is the size of the air's upward force on her, in newtons?

mistakes.why: Value: a steady speed means the air's push balances the weight, not that it vanishes.

why.correct: Steady speed means zero net force, so the air pushes up exactly as hard as Earth pulls down: F_air = mg = 60 kg × 9.8 m/s² = 590 N (588 N rounded to two significant figures).

items.q: An inertial reference frame is one in which
options: zero net force means constant velocity
each object stays at rest
there is no gravity acting
the observer is speeding up steadily

why.correct: The first law holds in an inertial frame, such as the ground or a train at constant velocity. In a speeding-up or braking vehicle, objects seem to lurch with no force on them.
options: Right: the first law holds there.
Objects can move in an inertial frame; they just keep constant velocity when the net force is zero.
Gravity acts in inertial frames too; it is a force with an agent.
A speeding-up observer is not in an inertial frame.
